readerTitle: The customers nobody rings a bell for
caseNote: 가상 사례 (팔레트 제조사, 클리닉 예약 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Reichheld & Sasser, 1990) · 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 신규 고객은 적자에서 출발한다. 이익은 남아 있는 고객에게서 나온다.
misconception: 성장은 신규 고객을 더 많이 데려오는 것이고, 마케팅·영업 예산을 늘리는 것이 가장 확실한 방법이다.

sources.text: Reichheld, F. F., & Sasser, W. E. (1990). Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services. Harvard Business Review.
팔레트 제조사와 클리닉 소프트웨어의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Reichheld & Sasser(1990)에 대해서는 '고객이 오래 머물수록 고객당 이익이 늘어나는 경향'만 일반적으로 적었습니다. 흔히 인용되는 '고객 유지율 5% 상승 시 이익 25~85%(또는 25~95%) 증가' 수치는 원문 확인 전에는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문에서 표현을 확인하세요.
'신규 고객 확보 비용이 기존 고객 유지보다 5~25배 비싸다' 같은 널리 퍼진 통계는 출처가 불분명해 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The customers nobody rings a bell for
body: At a regional pallet maker, the sales team rings a bell every time they sign a new account. This year they rang it 10 times.
Over the same year, 8 old customers quietly stopped ordering. Nobody rang anything for that. And those 8 were worth more than the 10 new ones.

image.label: Sales team cheering at a bell while customers leave through a back door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공장 사무실 앞쪽에서 영업팀이 종을 치며 환호하고, 뒤쪽 창고 문으로 팔레트를 실은 트럭 몇 대가 조용히 빠져나가는 장면. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where does the next $30,000 go?
body: You run the pallet maker. You have 40 business customers. About 8 leave each year, and most leave after late deliveries.
You have $30,000 to spend next year. What do you fund?

options.text: A part-time salesperson to win about 10 new accounts
options.feedback: New accounts matter, but each costs about $3,000 to win and won't pay that back this year. You'd be refilling what late deliveries drain.

options.text: Fix late deliveries: a backup truck and an extra shift in peak weeks
options.feedback: You protect customers who already trust you and already order at full size. The next card shows why that's worth more.

options.text: Give new customers 15% off their first three months
options.feedback: It may bring in buyers, but it shrinks what each new account earns and does nothing about why old ones leave.

cards.title: Follow one new account.
body: A new account loses money in year one and turns a small profit in year two, if it stays. Meanwhile, keeping 5 of the 8 customers who would leave is worth **$12,500 a year**, with no cost to win them.

breakdown.label: Cost to win
breakdown.detail: Sales visits, samples, a trial run

breakdown.label: Year 2
breakdown.detail: Full orders once they trust you

breakdown.label: After two years
breakdown.detail: Only if they don't leave first

cards.title: Why retention beats acquisition
body: **Retention** means keeping the customers you have. **Acquisition** means winning new ones.

Winning a customer costs money up front. The profit arrives later, a little with every order. A customer who leaves early may never pay back what you spent. A customer who stays is already paid for, so each new order adds profit.

image.label: Line dipping below zero, then rising year after year
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프. x축 "Years with you", y축 "Profit from one customer". 선이 처음에 0 아래로 내려갔다가("Cost to win") 해마다 위로 올라감. 중간에 끊긴 점선 하나는 "Left early" 라벨로 0 아래에서 멈춤.

cards.title: Kept customers get more valuable.
body: Frederick Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser described this pattern in a 1990 Harvard Business Review article, *Zero Defections*. In the service businesses they studied, profit per customer tended to grow the longer a customer stayed. Four reasons:
list: **No new cost to win:** you paid it once
**Bigger orders:** trust grows, so they buy more
**Cheaper to serve:** they know your process, you know their needs
**Referrals:** satisfied buyers send others your way

cards.title: Anywhere customers buy more than once.
body: A café regular costs nothing to attract again tomorrow. An accountant's ten-year client needs no onboarding this year. A repair shop's loyal fleet customer books without a quote.
The pattern holds wherever people can buy again. The first sale pays for winning them. The later sales pay for everything else.
cards.softwareNote: In subscription software, the cost to win a customer is mostly paid in month one, while revenue arrives monthly. A user who cancels in month two may never cover what the ads and demos cost.

cards.title: Not every customer is worth keeping.
body: Some customers cost more to serve than they pay: constant rush orders, late payments, endless custom work. Keeping them at any price is not a win. Neither is buying loyalty with discounts that teach everyone to threaten to leave.
And a business with no new customers slowly shrinks, because some will always leave for reasons you can't control. Retention comes first, not instead of acquisition.

cards.title: Now it's clinic software.
body: You sell scheduling software to small clinics for a monthly fee. Ads and sales demos cost about four months of fees to win each clinic.
Many clinics cancel in month two or three, saying setup was confusing. Your team has one quarter. What do they work on?

options.text: Features prospects ask for in sales demos
options.feedback: It could win more deals, but new clinics would hit the same confusing setup and leave before paying back what you spent.

options.text: Guided setup and a check-in call in the first month
options.feedback: Each clinic that stays past month four has covered its cost to win. Every month after that is profit.

options.text: Double the ad budget to outrun the cancellations
options.feedback: You'd pay four months of fees for clinics that stay two or three. More ads would grow the loss, not the business.

cards.title: Profit lives in the customers who stay.
body: Winning a customer is a cost. Keeping them is how that cost pays off.
**Try it today:** list the last five customers who stopped buying from you. Next to each, write why they left and roughly what it cost to win them.
